evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing insight and inspiration from our comrade Aziz Choudry, in this paper, we explore the role of political education and knowledge making in social movement struggles to contest the state and capital around access to water and other public services.

From 2007 until their phasing out in mid-2021, WMDs were a key component of the City of Cape Town’s (CoCT) water demand management strategy and have been at the centre of struggles over water in the city.
And the bureaucratic process for indigent status and exclusionary eligibility requirements remains.
I have spent the last decade working alongside Faeza, Ebrahiem and many others in struggles around public services in Cape Town.
We continue to organise to protect and defend our communities from this latest intervention and propose an alternative: ‘Water for Life’.

criterion_notes.c1: Discusses household and community water service access, restriction, and affordability in working-class areas and informal settlements in Cape Town as the substantive context of water-justice activism.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading at a topical level: the paper discusses municipal cost-recovery rules, indigent-status eligibility requirements, Free Basic Water volume caps, rising block tariffs, Water Management Devices (WMDs), and punitive trickle-flow restricting discs and prepaid meters. However, these mechanisms are described only through secondary policy commentary as background to activist political education rather than examined empirically, so the overall study decision remains exclude under both readings.
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical research methodology, systematic data collection, or primary empirical data on water access (and not a systematic empirical synthesis). The article is a reflective activist-scholar essay combining three autobiographical 'Personal Learning Hi(stories)', Marxist pedagogical theory (drawing on Choudry and Allman), narrative reflections on movement 'water mapping' workshops, and a secondary-source policy overview -> exclude as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not report primary empirical outcomes on household or community water access; statistics and tariff/cutoff figures are cited solely from secondary reports and news sources (e.g., StatsSA, CoCT reports, GroundUp, Ruiters), while the authors' own narrative focuses on political consciousness and movement solidarity.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, sampling frame, or unit-of-analysis empirical dataset linking a governance exposure to a service-access outcome.

exposure: Municipal water demand management and cost-recovery rules discussed via secondary policy sources (Free Basic Water allocations, indigent status eligibility, rising block tariffs, Water Management Devices, and trickle-flow restricting discs), alongside activist political education workshops
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the paper discusses Cape Town water service access (c1) and rule-type municipal mechanisms such as indigent eligibility requirements, Free Basic Water allowances, rising block tariffs, Water Management Devices, and flow-restricting discs (c2), it is a theoretical and autobiographical activist-scholar essay on political education and movement praxis combined with a secondary-source policy overview. It reports no empirical study design, no systematic primary data collection or sample, and no primary empirical evidence on household or community water-access outcomes (c3, c4, c5).
